findings.title: Broken parent and dependency references point at documents that do not exist
findings.description: Frontmatter declares `dependsOn: [001-concept.migratory, 100-arch.behavior-engine]` and Related Work links `../project-guides/001-concept.migratory.md`. The actual concept is `project-documents/user/project-guides/000-concept.migratory.md`; `001` is `001-initiative-plan.migratory.md`. Every substantive claim in "Motivation" and "Current State" ("The concept document establishes that 'the world is the primary artifact…'", "These technology choices are established in the concept document") therefore cites a document that is not the one linked. The mirror problem exists in `100-arch.behavior-engine.md:122` and `100-slices.behavior-engine.md:43`, which reference `200-arch.world-server-foundation.md` — no such file; this doc is numbered `300`. Since these docs are navigated by AI agents via frontmatter and relative links, the dangling `200`-vs-`300` mismatch means the behavior engine's interface requirements ("must not preclude aggregation") are cited from a path that resolves to nothing. Fix the index in both directions before (304)/(305) design work inherits the wrong cross-references.

findings.title: The architecture owns the environment layer; the slice plan and initiative plan do not
findings.description: "Scope" lists "environment hosting" as the server's responsibility, and "Envisioned State" says "The environment layer is hosted within the server process and provides terrain elevation, biome data, resource locations, and seasonal state." "Configuration surface" requires the server to own "environment parameters (terrain seed, biome layout, seasonal cycle length)", and "Anticipated Slices" includes both "Environment layer foundation" (terrain generation, resource placement) and "Seasonal and temporal systems." But `300-slices.worldserver-foundation.md` slice (304) states "The environment layer itself — terrain, biomes, resources, seasonal logic — is owned by initiative 500," and (308) splits temporal ownership ("The server owns *when* time advances… What seasons *mean* is owned by initiative 500"). `001-initiative-plan.migratory.md` makes 500 a separate initiative that depends on 300. The architecture document — which is the normative parent for the slice plan — still describes the environment as built here. Also note `dateUpdated: 20260318` predates the initiative plan (20260329) and slice plan update (20260401), which explains the drift but does not resolve it. As written, an implementer following the arch doc will build terrain generation inside `migratory_server` while (304) expects to consume it from a 500 package. This must be rewritten to the orchestrator/hand-off boundary before (304) is specced, or the two will diverge.

findings.title: "Read-only" environment interface precludes stigmergy, yet slice 304 requires writes
findings.description: The environment is specified as "provides… a read-only query interface" to the behavior engine, and environment data "is generated or loaded at startup." This is not a neutral choice: it structurally excludes the "Swarm intelligence" archetype from the concept ("stigmergic coordination through the environment… paths reinforced through use"), which `100-arch.behavior-engine.md` also lists as a first-class archetype. And `300-slices.worldserver-foundation.md` (304) already contradicts it: "Handle post-tick environment writes (e.g., stigmergic trail deposits)." So the server is required to perform a write path the architecture forbids, and the document never says who owns it — the engine writing back through the server's tick, the environment mutating itself during `environment.update()` (step 2 of the core loop, before behavior evaluation, which cannot see this tick's deposits), or the server translating engine output into environment writes. This is a boundary in the wrong place, not merely a missing detail: step ordering in the "Envisioned State" (environment update → behavior evaluation → commit) hard-codes a one-way flow. Also flag that `100-arch.behavior-engine.md`'s "Environment as input surface" principle shares the defect, so the two docs need a coordinated fix rather than a local patch.

findings.title: The tick/asyncio coexistence strategy is wrong as stated and cannot service I/O
findings.description:
The stated mechanism — "run the tick synchronously, then yield to the async event loop for I/O between ticks" — does not deliver what "Between ticks, the server handles client connections" requires. Two concrete problems, both verifiable in `src/migratory_server/tick.py`:

1. Awaiting a coroutine whose body is entirely synchronous never yields to the event loop. `TickLoop.run()` does `await self._tick_body(...)`, and `server.py`'s `tick_body` calls `sim.step()` with no `await` inside it. So the tick holds the loop for its full duration, and client I/O is serviced only at `asyncio.sleep(remaining)`.
2. On overrun the loop takes the `remaining < 0` branch, logs a warning, and **skips the sleep entirely** — so the event loop is not run between consecutive overruns at all. The stated degradation policy ("warn on overrun, continue at best effort") is precisely the case where client connections starve, and the doc's own "handle slow or stalled clients without blocking the tick loop" goal is violated by the escalation path rather than protected from it.

The stated upgrade path ("offloading the tick to a thread or process (NumPy releases the GIL)") also does not fit the actual hot path: `src/migratory/engine/tick.py` builds neighbor lists with a Python `for idx in eval_indices:` loop plus per-agent `np.linalg.norm`/`np.where` allocations, which holds the GIL for the dominant cost — a thread gets no parallelism there. And a *process* offload contradicts the design goal "Single-process simplicity — no inter-process communication" and the engine's "stateless between ticks — all state lives in the arrays passed to it," because `tick()` mutates `state` in place; crossing a process boundary each tick means serializing the full SoA set every tick, a cost the doc's egress arithmetic (12 bytes/entity) does not model. The document needs to pick the real mechanism: a separate executor with a bounded queue and an explicit state-hand-off copy, or accept that ticks block I/O and define the maximum tolerable tick time. Note also that this is already partially built, so the doc's vagueness is now a live design debt rather than a future question.

findings.title: Entity memory and removal cost are understated because the ID layer is ignored
findings.description:
"The system's entity capacity is bounded by three resources in this order: spatial query cost, network egress, and raw computation. Memory is never the constraint (500K entities ≈ 24MB…)". That figure counts only the SoA arrays (positions + velocities + accelerations as float64 plus int32 profile indices ≈ 52 bytes/entity). It omits the entity-identity layer the architecture itself mandates ("The server assigns entity IDs"), which in `src/migratory_server/entities.py` is two Python `dict[int,int]` mappings (`_id_to_index`, `_index_to_id`). In CPython, a dict of 500K int→int entries is on the order of tens of MB *each*, i.e. the identity bookkeeping exceeds the state arrays it is claimed to be negligible next to — so "memory is never the constraint" is false for the design as specified, and the ordering of constraints (memory last) is wrong at the upper tiers.

Related and more load-bearing: the doc says "Entity capacity determines array pre-allocation sizes," but there is no pre-allocation anywhere in the design. `AgentState.create(n, …)` allocates exactly `n` rows; `add_agent` and `spawn_population` grow via `np.concatenate` (full copy per spawn), and `remove_entity` does a Python `np.delete` on four arrays *plus* an O(active) rebuild of both ID dictionaries with index shifting. At 10K entities and the spawn/removal churn the doc anticipates ("Handle entity lifecycle events (spawning, removals, profile changes) queued during the tick"), this is a per-tick O(n) copy path that the scaling section never accounts for — and it directly undermines the "10K–50K comfortable on a single CPU" claim, which is stated as though the only costs were spatial queries and forces. The architecture should specify either a free-list / compaction strategy with pre-allocated capacity, or an explicit "indices are not stable; consumers use IDs" contract. As written it promises pre-allocation and delivers reallocation.

findings.title: Float64 state vs. Float32 wire/GPU format: the conversion cost is unaddressed where the doc makes its egress claim
findings.description: "State representation and serialization" says "Raw float buffers are compact and fast" and the scaling section computes 500K entities at "12 bytes each" (which implies float32: 2+2 floats × 4B). But the arrays are float64 (`src/migratory/engine/state.py`: `dtype=np.float64`), so 4 positions+velocities floats = 32 bytes/entity — egress is 2.7× the doc's figure at the same entity count. `100-arch.behavior-engine.md` explicitly identifies this tension ("The concept specifies Float32Array for transfer and GPU upload, while float64 may be preferred for simulation precision — the engine should define its internal precision and provide an efficient conversion path at the serialization boundary"). The world server doc, which owns serialization, states no precision decision and no conversion step, and never mentions the copy/convert cost per tick per client. Since the doc's own scaling wall #2 is "network egress," getting the element size wrong is not cosmetic. Decision needed: internal precision, boundary conversion owner (server, not engine), and whether the 24MB/12 bytes-per-entity figures are re-derived.

findings.title: Replay from initial state requires deterministic spawn RNG; the doc names "environment seed" but no world/entity seed
findings.description:
"Logging format and replay fidelity" asserts that if the tick function is deterministic, "logging only the initial state plus any non-deterministic inputs (entity spawns/removals, configuration changes) is sufficient." Two gaps make this claim unusable as a spec:

1. The only seed in the architecture's config list is the *environment* seed. There is no entity-population seed. "Configuration surface" lists "entity population definitions (which profiles, how many, where)" — and `spawn_population` in the implementation draws random positions from `np.random.default_rng()` with no seed and no config field (`config/default.yaml` has no seed key, and `spawn_population(pop)` is called without `rng` from `server.py`). So the initial spawn positions — part of "the initial state" the log says it will reconstruct — are non-reproducible across a restart, defeating "given a log and the same configuration, the simulation can be reconstructed tick-by-tick."
2. If instead spawn positions are treated as "non-deterministic inputs" to be logged, then the log must record every spawned entity's exact position *and assigned ID*. The doc never says the log captures entity IDs, and IDs matter because removal compacts indices: without an ID→position record, a replayed spawn sequence produces a different index layout, and delta encoding computed against a live index space breaks. The doc lists "ID assignment" as an entity-management concern but never connects IDs to serialization, replay, or the snapshot/delta decision. This is the "step 3: magic happens" of the replay feature and needs to be written down before slice (307).

findings.title: The wire protocol is described only as entity-state framing, but the design requires multiple payload types
findings.description: The protocol is specified as "a minimal framing protocol (tick number, entity count, array layout descriptor) wrapping raw buffers." That schema carries exactly one message kind. The document's own requirements need at least four: (a) connect-time full snapshot, which per slice (305) must include "world bounds, entity positions/velocities, terrain summary"; (b) ongoing tick state; (c) optional deltas — the doc says "clients may receive deltas for efficiency, or full snapshots if the delta approach proves premature," leaving the decision open, yet a delta requires an anchor/reference the framing has no field for; (d) log records, which the doc says use the same serialization ("Logging captures simulation state… the log format supports replay"). Endianness, float precision, and how the "array layout descriptor" represents aggregate entities (introduced later in the same section as a first-class entity kind with a different shape — center of mass, heading, dispersion, count) are all unspecified. Note also an internal inconsistency: "No client-to-server simulation commands exist in v1, though the protocol should not preclude adding them later" — a tick-prefixed entity-buffer frame with no message-type field cannot be extended to client commands or handshake replies without a format change, which is exactly the kind of rearchitecting the doc elsewhere tries to avoid. Finally, slice (306) puts serialization *after* (305) WebSocket Client Layer as a dependency of it, which means clients get built against an undesigned protocol; the architecture should reverse or merge that ordering.

findings.title: No component decomposition or interface contracts, despite "Orchestrator, not monolith" being a stated principle
findings.description: The document enumerates responsibilities ("Scope": server lifecycle, tick loop, entity management, environment hosting, client connection management, serialization, configuration, logging) and asserts "The world server coordinates the behavior engine, environment layer, and client layer through well-defined interfaces," but never defines any interface, module, or boundary of the server's *own* internals. Specifically missing: (1) the interface between entity management and the engine's `AgentState` — who owns the index↔ID map, and is the engine allowed to reorder or compact rows? (2) the contract for the init-hook extension point that slice (300) actually built (`register_init_hook`/`register_shutdown_hook`) — the architecture says "The server knows how to initialize subsystems in order" but never states the order or its constraints (must environment exist before entity spawn? must spatial indexing receive world bounds before the first tick? slice (303) says yes, the arch doc does not). (3) the tick-body composition contract — the six-step core loop is prose, not an interface, so each integration slice edits the same function. The consequence is visible in `server.py`, where `run()` wires config → profiles → `EntityManager` → populations → `SimulationManager` → `BruteForceQuery` → `TickLoop` inline, with the spatial strategy hard-coded in the lifecycle method rather than injected. That is the monolith the principle was meant to prevent, and it also means the tick-loop ordering is an implicit shared resource: the slice plan Notes claim (304) and (305) are independent and parallelizable, but both touch the same ordered tick body that the architecture never modularized. "Subsystem orchestration, not subsystem reimplementation" needs a component list to mean anything.

findings.title: Client failure policy and the observability goal are both left undecided
findings.description: Two sections defer the actual decision: "Client connection lifecycle" lists "buffering, dropping frames, or disconnecting unresponsive clients are all strategies to consider" — no criteria, no threshold, and no statement of what the client is told when it is silently desynchronized (which conflicts with the project rule against silent fallbacks; a dropped frame with no sequence gap indicator leaves the client rendering stale state believing it is current). "Graceful degradation under load" resolves to "warn on overrun, continue at best effort, and provide metrics to diagnose the bottleneck," but no metrics are defined: "Observable by default" is a Design Goal ("The server is designed to be watched. Client connections, state streaming, and logging are first-class concerns"), yet observability appears nowhere in the Scope list, no component owns it, and the implementation's metrics are a bare mutable `TickMetrics` dataclass read by nothing. Under-specified here means (305) will invent its own buffer policy and (307) will invent its own counters, which is the divergence the architecture exists to prevent. The doc also never addresses shutdown semantics for the client layer: "drain client connections gracefully" is asserted, but there is no final-state frame, no in-flight-write flush ordering for the log relative to client drain, and no behavior defined for a client connected during the tick that triggers shutdown.

findings.title: Scaling prose for 500K–4M+ entities is disproportionate to this architecture's remit and self-contradictory
findings.description: "Technical Considerations" is dominated by entity-scaling content that the plan explicitly does not build: tiers through 4M+ entities, "CuPy or custom CUDA kernels," "multi-GPU with dynamic spatial partitioning," predictive partition rebalancing, and temporary aggregation elevation for merging murmurations. Yet `001-initiative-plan.migratory.md` defers all of it to initiative 620 ("deliberately deferred — it could expand the product scope 5-fold or more"), and `300-slices.worldserver-foundation.md` moves multi-resolution simulation out of the feature slices entirely into Future Work at "Risk: High, Effort: 4/5," noting "implementing aggregation itself is future work." The document contradicts its own goal ("no distribution infrastructure is built until it is needed") and its own concession ("The architecture should not prescribe a solution but must ensure the entity management and tick loop designs do not preclude these approaches") by prescribing five paragraphs of non-solution. **What to cut here:** the 1M–4M and 4M+ tiers, the GPU/CUDA specifics, the group-encounter strategy menu, and the multi-GPU escalation path — all of which belong in the (deferred) 620 initiative, and are already captured in interface form on the engine side (`100-arch.behavior-engine.md`'s subset-evaluable tick and pluggable spatial query principles). **What should replace them:** the short, checkable list of constraints this architecture must actually satisfy *now* — which the doc never states — (a) entity index space must not be assumed stable by clients or logs, (b) the tick interface must accept an evaluation subset, (c) the entity model must admit a second entity kind with a different attribute shape for aggregates, (d) serialization must version the array layout descriptor. Meanwhile the concrete v1 hard parts (tick/async mechanism, environment write-back, protocol types, replay determinism, client policy — above) get one line each. Rebalancing in that direction is the change worth making; it is also the cheapest, since it is prose and decision list, not code.

findings.title: Profile configuration ownership is unclaimed between 300 and 100
findings.description: "Single-process simplicity" and "Profile-driven behavior" both assume profiles come from server configuration ("Entities are created from behavioral profiles defined in configuration"), and `100-arch.behavior-engine.md` says profiles "can be serialized, loaded from configuration, and swapped at runtime" while keeping the parameter set (weights, ranges, thresholds, separation radius, per-archetype knobs) as the engine's concern. The world server doc never states whether it owns the profile *schema*, validates it, or treats it as an opaque pass-through — nor whether runtime profile swapping (an engine capability) is a server responsibility, since the server owns entity lifecycle. This ambiguity has already produced a concrete break: `src/migratory_server/simulation.py:build_profiles` constructs `BehavioralProfile(max_speed=…, query_radius=…)` from a `ProfileConfig` that has only those three fields, while `src/migratory/engine/profile.py` requires six (cohesion/separation/alignment weights and separation_radius have no defaults) — and `config/default.yaml` correspondingly exposes only `name`/`max_speed`/`query_radius`. The stated server capability "create initial entity populations from configured profiles" therefore does not currently work end-to-end. Fix the ownership sentence in the architecture (recommendation: server owns transport/validation of an opaque profile document, engine owns the schema and interpretation) and the slice will fall out of it.

findings.title: Frontmatter status and content lag the delivered work
findings.description: `status: in_progress` with `dateUpdated: 20260318`, while slices 300–303 are checked off, verified against a walkthrough (slice 300's "Verified 2026-03-25"), and running in `src/`. "Current State: No world server exists" is now false — a server with lifecycle, config, tick loop, entity management, and engine integration exists, using `BruteForceQuery` (not the spatial hash the scaling section assumes) and a hard-wired `forces=[]` list. The Architecture Principle "Tick as transaction — read current state, compute next state, commit" also does not match the implemented loop: `tick()` mutates `AgentState` in place (`src/migratory/engine/tick.py` docstring: "mutated in place"), so there is no "commit" and no ability to discard a tick, which is what "atomic operation" and "between ticks, the world is consistent and queryable" promise — and what the deferred snapshot-isolation for client reads would need. Either update Current State, or state that the principle is a target rather than a property of the current implementation; as written an agent reading it will believe both that nothing exists and that ticks are atomic.
